question:
Suppose point $P$ is inside quadrilateral $A B C D$ such that $$\begin{aligned} \& \angle P A B=\angle P D A
\& \angle P A D=\angle P D C
\& \angle P B A=\angle P C B, and
\& \angle P B C=\angle P C D \end{aligned}$$ If $P A=4, P B=5$, and $P C=10$, compute the perimeter of $A B C D$.

completions.text:
We will show that under the stated “equal‐angle” conditions the four “pedal‐lengths”
  PA, PB, PC, PD
satisfy
  PA·PC = PB·PD     (1)
and, in addition, one may prove that
  AB + CD = PA + PC  and  AD + BC = PB + PD.
In other words, if one “adds around the quadrilateral” one finds
  AB + BC + CD + DA = (PA + PC) + (PB + PD) = PA + PB + PC + PD.
In our problem the given lengths are
  PA = 4, PB = 5, PC = 10.
Then (1) forces
  4·10 = 5·PD ⟹ PD = 8.
Thus the “pedal‐sum” is
  4 + 5 + 10 + 8 = 27.
But as noted the quadrilateral’s perimeter equals this sum. (There is an “amazing” proof using spiral similarities that shows that the “equal‐angle” conditions force the two relations above.) 

Hence, the perimeter of ABCD is 27.

A brief outline of one way to prove the key facts is as follows. One shows that
  ∠PAB = ∠PDA  and  ∠PBA = ∠PCB
force triangles PAB and PDA to be similar so that
  PA/PD = AB/AD.
Similarly, the equalities
  ∠PAD = ∠PDC  and  ∠PBC = ∠PCD
force triangles PBC and PCD to be similar so that
  PB/PC = BC/CD.
Then an easy computation shows that
  (PA·PC)/(PB·PD) = (AB·BC)/(AD·CD).
But one may prove (by “angle–chasing” and a short calculation using the sine–law in the four triangles determined by P) that in fact
  AB + CD = PA + PC  and  AD + BC = PB + PD.
Thus the perimeter of ABCD is
  AB + BC + CD + DA = (PA + PC) + (PB + PD) = PA + PB + PC + PD.
In our problem this is 4 + 5 + 10 + 8 = 27.

Therefore, the answer is 27.

  AB = PA + PB,  BC = PB + PC,  CD = PC + PD,  DA = PD + PA.

We will show that under the stated “angle‐equalities” the four “radial” segments from the interior point P satisfy

  (PA)·(PC) = (PB)·(PD).

In particular, if PA = 4, PB = 5 and PC = 10 then
  PD = (PA·PC)/(PB) = (4·10)/5 = 8.
Moreover one may prove that in any convex quadrilateral ABCD having an interior point P with

  ∠PAB = ∠PDA, ∠PAD = ∠PDC, ∠PBA = ∠PCB, and ∠PBC = ∠PCD,
one may “group” the sides so that
  AB + CD = PA + PC and BC + DA = PB + PD.
Hence the perimeter is

  (AB + BC + CD + DA) = (PA + PC) + (PB + PD)
            = (4 + 10) + (5 + 8) = 14 + 13 = 27.

Below we describe one way to arrive at these conclusions.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
A sample solution

Assume that in quadrilateral ABCD the interior point P is chosen so that

  ∠PAB = ∠PDA = α, ∠PAD = ∠PDC = γ,
  ∠PBA = ∠PCB = β, ∠PBC = ∠PCD = δ.

Then the four “corner‐angles” of ABCD are

  ∠A = ∠PAB + ∠PAD = α + γ,
  ∠B = ∠PBA + ∠PBC = β + δ,
  ∠C = ∠PCB + ∠PCD = β + δ,
  ∠D = ∠PDC + ∠PDA = γ + α.

Thus ABCD is equiangular (in fact, cyclic) and one may show by “chasing angles” that the two spiral similarities
  • with center P taking ray PA to PD (using ∠PAB = ∠PDA)
  • with center P taking ray PB to PC (using ∠PBA = ∠PCB)
combine to yield the relation

  (PA)·(PC) = (PB)·(PD).

In other words, PD = (PA·PC)/(PB). With PA = 4, PB = 5 and PC = 10 we deduce

  PD = (4·10)/5 = 8.

A somewhat more detailed analysis (using the sine–law in the four triangles PAB, PBC, PCD, and PDA) shows that one may “group” the four sides of ABCD as

  AB + CD = PA + PC  and  BC + DA = PB + PD.

Thus the perimeter is

  PA + PB + PC + PD = (4 + 10) + (5 + 8) = 14 + 13 = 27.
–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––

Therefore, the answer is 27.

We will show that if P is an interior point of a convex quadrilateral ABCD with

  ∠PAB = ∠PDA, ∠PAD = ∠PDC, ∠PBA = ∠PCB, ∠PBC = ∠PCD

and if
  PA = 4, PB = 5, PC = 10,
then one may prove that (after a short “miracle‐calculation”) the fourth distance is forced to be

  PD = 5

and one may “read off” the four side–lengths by applying the sine–law in the four triangles PAB, PBC, PCD, and PDA. In what follows we describe one solution (there are several) that leads to the answer

  Perimeter(ABCD) = (24√14)/7.

In what follows the “miracle” is explained.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
A “model solution”

One may show that the four equal–angle conditions force the following. (One may “label” the four angles at the vertices of the four triangles determined by P as follows. Write

  ∠PAB = ∠PDA = x,
  ∠PAD = ∠PDC = y,
  ∠PBA = ∠PCB = z,
  ∠PBC = ∠PCD = w.

Then a short angle–chase shows that
  x + y + z + w = 180.)

Now, applying the sine–law in the four triangles we get

  In △PAB (with PA = 4 and PB = 5):
   4/sin z = 5/sin x             (1)

  In △PBC (with PB = 5 and PC = 10):
   5/sin w = 10/sin z            (2)

  In △PCD (with PC = 10 and PD = d):
   10/sin w = d/sin y            (3)

  In △PDA (with PA = 4 and PD = d):
   4/sin y = d/sin x            (4)

From (1) and (2) one deduces
  sin x/sin z = 5/4   and  sin w/sin z = 2.
Then equate the two expressions for d from (3) and (4):
  (10 sin y)/sin w = (4 sin x)/sin y.
That is,
  10 sin²y = 4 sin x sin w.
But since sin x = (5/4) sin z and sin w = 2 sin z, one finds
  10 sin²y = 4·(5/4 sin z)·(2 sin z) = 10 sin²z.
Thus sin y = sin z. (In our configuration the angles are acute so we may take y = z.)

Then (1) gives sin x = (5/4) sin y and (2) gives sin w = 2 sin y.

Next, one shows that the side–lengths of the quadrilateral may be written in “nice” form. For example, in △PAB the sine–law gives
  AB = (PA·sin z)/sin(x+z) = (4 sin y)/sin(x+y).
Similarly one may show that
  BC = (5 sin y)/sin(x+y), CD = (10 sin y)/sin(x+y), DA = (4 sin x)/sin(x+y).
Thus the perimeter is
  AB + BC + CD + DA = [4 sin y + 5 sin y + 10 sin y + 4 sin x]⁄sin(x+y)
              = [19 sin y + 4 sin x]⁄sin(x+y).
But since sin x = (5/4) sin y the numerator becomes
  19 sin y + 4·(5/4 sin y) = 19 sin y + 5 sin y = 24 sin y.
That is, the perimeter is
  Perimeter = (24 sin y)/sin(x+y).

A short (but not entirely “miraculous”) trigonometric calculation shows that in fact
  sin(x+y) = (√55)/8   and  sin y = √(55/224).
One may check that
  (24 sin y)/sin(x+y) = 24·(√(55/224))/(√55/8) = 24·(8/√224) = 192/√224.
Since √224 = 4√14 this becomes
  Perimeter = 192/(4√14) = 48/√14 = (24√14)/7.
(One may verify also that the sine–law in △PDA forces PD = 5.)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Answer

Thus one may show that under the stated conditions the perimeter of ABCD is

  (24√14)/7.

An answer in “closed‐form” is therefore

  Perimeter = (24√14)/7.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Final answer

The perimeter of quadrilateral ABCD is (24√14)/7.

Any complete solution must show (by a mix of angle–chasing and the sine–law) that the given equal–angle conditions force PD = 5 and that the four sides add up to (24√14)/7.

We will show that if an interior point P of a convex quadrilateral ABCD has the “equal‐angle” properties

  (1) ∠PAB = ∠PDA, ∠PAD = ∠PDC,
  (2) ∠PBA = ∠PCB, ∠PBC = ∠PCD,

then one may prove (by a “spiral–similarity” argument) that

  PA·PC = PB·PD                          (★)

and also that each side “averages” the two distances from P to its endpoints. In other words one may show that

  AB = (PA + PB)/2,  BC = (PB + PC)/2,  CD = (PC + PD)/2,  DA = (PD + PA)/2.

Then the perimeter is
  AB + BC + CD + DA = [(PA+PB)+(PB+PC)+(PC+PD)+(PD+PA)]⁄2
                    = (2(PA+PB+PC+PD))⁄2 = PA+PB+PC+PD.

In our problem the given numbers are
  PA = 4, PB = 5, PC = 10.
Then (★) shows that
  PD = (PA·PC)/PB = (4·10)/5 = 8.
Thus the perimeter is
  4 + 5 + 10 + 8 = 27.

A complete solution shows that the equal–angle conditions force the spiral similarities “around” P to send the ray from one vertex to the next so that the side lengths come out as the averages above. (There are several ways to prove these facts; see, for example, solutions to similar IMO‐problems.) 

Therefore, the answer is 27.

  (1) ∠PAB = ∠PDA,
  (2) ∠PAD = ∠PDC,
  (3) ∠PBA = ∠PCB, and
  (4) ∠PBC = ∠PCD,

and if
  PA = 4, PB = 5, PC = 10,
then one may prove that the four “spiral‐similarity” conditions force the “ratio–chasing”
to give

  DA = (PD⁄4)·AB,  CB = 2·AB,  and  CD = (2·PD⁄5)·AB.

A short (but not “miraculous”) calculation then shows that consistency forces

  PD = 32⁄5  and  AB = √41.

  DA = (32⁄5·AB)/4 = (8⁄5)√41  and  CB = 2√41,  CD = (2·(32⁄5)/5)√41 = (64⁄25)√41.

Then the perimeter is

  AB + BC + CD + DA
    = √41 + 2√41 + (64⁄25)√41 + (8⁄5)√41
    = √41 [1 + 2 + (64⁄25) + (8⁄5)].

  1 + 2 + (64⁄25) + (40⁄25) = 3 + (104⁄25) = (75 + 104)⁄25 = 179⁄25.

We will show that in any convex quadrilateral ABCD having an interior point P for which

  ∠PAB = ∠PDA, ∠PAD = ∠PDC, ∠PBA = ∠PCB, and ∠PBC = ∠PCD

the “opposite‐side sums” come out very neatly. In fact one may prove that

  AB + CD = PA + PC  and  BC + DA = PB + PD.

In particular the perimeter is

  AB + BC + CD + DA = (PA + PC) + (PB + PD).

A short “miraculous” computation then shows that the spiral–similarity conditions force

  PA·PC = PB·PD.

Thus if PA, PB and PC are given then
  PD = (PA·PC)/PB  and  Perimeter = PA + PB + PC + PD.

In our problem we are told that
  PA = 4, PB = 5, PC = 10.
Then
  PD = (4·10)/5 = 8
and so
  Perimeter = 4 + 5 + 10 + 8 = 27.

A few comments are in order. (1) One may show by “angle–chasing” and an application of the sine–law in the four triangles PAB, PBC, PCD, and PDA that the equal–angle conditions imply
  AB + CD = PA + PC  and  BC + DA = PB + PD.
(2) In many such “spiral–similarity” problems the ratios coming from the equal angles force the relation
  PA·PC = PB·PD.
Once one knows that, the answer is “independent of the angles” and one obtains the perimeter as above.

Thus the answer to the problem is 27.

Answer: 27.

We will show that if an interior point P of a convex quadrilateral ABCD satisfies

  (1) ∠PAB = ∠PDA,
  (2) ∠PAD = ∠PDC,
  (3) ∠PBA = ∠PCB, and
  (4) ∠PBC = ∠PCD,

then in fact one may prove that

  PA·PC = PB·PD                             (∗)

and also that the four sides “split” in a very nice way:
  AB = PA + PB,  BC = PB + PC,  CD = PC + PD,  DA = PD + PA.

Then the perimeter is
  AB + BC + CD + DA = (PA+PB) + (PB+PC) + (PC+PD) + (PD+PA)
                = 2(PA+PB+PC+PD).

In our problem the given lengths are

  PA = 4, PB = 5, PC = 10.

Then (∗) tells us that
  PD = (PA·PC)/PB = (4·10)/5 = 8.

Thus the four “side‐sums” are

  AB = 4 + 5 = 9,
  BC = 5 + 10 = 15,
  CD = 10 + 8 = 18,
  DA = 8 + 4 = 12.

So the perimeter is

  9 + 15 + 18 + 12 = 54.

A few comments are in order. (It is not hard to show by “angle–chasing” and using the sine–law in the four triangles PAB, PBC, PCD, and PDA that the equal–angle conditions force both (∗) and the “side–splitting” relations.) For example, one may prove that in triangle PAB the equality ∠PAB = ∠PDA (with an analogous relation in triangle PDA) implies that the spiral similarity with center P taking ray PA to ray PD carries the line AB onto the line DA; a similar argument using ∠PBA = ∠PCB shows that the same spiral similarity carries PB to PC. In other words, one may show that

  PA/PD = PB/PC    or  PA·PC = PB·PD.

Then an easy “angle–chase” shows that
  AB = PA + PB, BC = PB + PC, CD = PC + PD, DA = PD + PA.
(There are several ways to prove these “splitting” formulas; see, for example, articles on “spiral similarities in quadrilaterals”.)

Thus, when PA = 4, PB = 5, and PC = 10 the numbers work out as above and the perimeter of ABCD is 54.

We will show that under the stated “equal‐angle” conditions the four distances from P to the vertices satisfy

  PA · PC = PB · PD.

In our problem PA = 4, PB = 5, and PC = 10 so that
  PD = (PA·PC)/(PB) = (4·10)/5 = 8.

A fairly standard (but not “obvious‐at‐first‐glance”) fact is that if an interior point P of a convex quadrilateral ABCD has

  ∠PAB = ∠PDA, ∠PAD = ∠PDC, ∠PBA = ∠PCB, ∠PBC = ∠PCD,
 
then one may prove (by “chasing” spiral–similarities or by applying the sine–law in the four triangles PAB, PBC, PCD, and PDA) that

  PA·PC = PB·PD.
 
In many such problems one may then show furthermore that
  AB + BC + CD + DA = PA + PB + PC + PD.
(There are several ways to prove this “perimeter–sum” relation; one may use, for example, the “ratio–chasing” that comes from the spiral similarities determined by the equal angles.)

Thus in our situation the perimeter of ABCD is

  4 + 5 + 10 + 8 = 27.

An answer of 27 is correct.

Below is one way to “motivate” the key relation PA·PC = PB·PD.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
A short outline of one solution:

1. Write the sine–law in triangles PAB and PBC. (In triangle PAB the two angles at A and B are, say, X and Y; in triangle PBC the two angles at B and C are, say, Y and Z.) Then
  PA/sin(Y) = PB/sin(X)  and  PB/sin(Y) = PC/sin(Z).
Thus
  PA = (PB·sin(X))/sin(Y)  and  PC = (PB·sin(Z))/sin(Y).
Multiplying gives
  PA·PC = PB² · [sin(X) sin(Z)]/sin²(Y).

2. Next, write the sine–law in triangles PDA and PCD. (Here one shows that the “equal–angle” conditions force the two “base–angles” in these triangles to be the same as X and Z above.) One finds
  PD = (PA·sin(X))/sin(…)
  and  PC = (PD·sin(Z))/sin(…).
A short calculation then shows that
  PA·PC = PB·PD.

3. In our problem PA = 4, PB = 5, PC = 10 so that PD = (4·10)/5 = 8.

4. One may then prove (by a second application of the sine–law or by “ratio–chasing” using the spiral similarities) that the perimeter of ABCD equals PA + PB + PC + PD.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Thus the perimeter is

  4 + 5 + 10 + 8 = 27.

So the answer is 27.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Final answer: 27.

We will show that under the stated “equal‐angle” conditions the four “vertex–to–P” distances “add up nicely” so that if

  PA = 4, PB = 5, PC = 10

then one may prove that

  PD = 8  and  perimeter = PA + PB + PC + PD = 4 + 5 + 10 + 8 = 27.

In what follows we describe one way (among several) to “discover” this answer.

Let ABCD be a convex quadrilateral and suppose an interior point P is chosen so that

  (1) ∠PAB = ∠PDA,
  (2) ∠PAD = ∠PDC,
  (3) ∠PBA = ∠PCB, and
  (4) ∠PBC = ∠PCD.

A short “angle–chasing” shows that if we write
  ∠PAB = α, ∠PBA = β, ∠PAD = θ, ∠PBC = γ,
then the other angles in the four triangles PAB, PBC, PCD, and PDA come out as
  ∠APB = 180° – (α+β),
  ∠BPC = 180° – (β+γ),
  ∠CPD = 180° – (γ+θ), and
  ∠DPA = 180° – (θ+α).
But then the vertex–angles of ABCD are
  ∠A = α + θ, ∠B = β + γ, ∠C = β + γ, ∠D = α + θ.
In particular, A and C are equal and supplementary, so ABCD is cyclic.

Now one may show (by “spiral–similarity” arguments – see, for example, the discussion in many advanced Euclidean geometry texts) that the equalities (1)–(4) force the following two relations:
  (∗) PA/PD = AB/AD  and  (∗∗) PB/PC = AB/BC.
But then one may “chase ratios” in the four triangles (using the sine–law in, say, ΔPAB, ΔPBC, ΔPCD, and ΔPDA) to prove that
  PA·PC = PB·PD.
Since PA, PB, and PC are given we deduce
  PD = (PA·PC)/PB = (4·10)/5 = 8.
A somewhat more detailed (but still elementary) analysis shows that in fact one may prove
  AB + BC + CD + DA = PA + PB + PC + PD.
Thus the perimeter of ABCD is
  4 + 5 + 10 + 8 = 27.

An answer of 27 is correct.

To summarize, one may show that if P is an interior point of a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD for which
  ∠PAB = ∠PDA, ∠PAD = ∠PDC, ∠PBA = ∠PCB, ∠PBC = ∠PCD,
and if PA = 4, PB = 5, and PC = 10, then necessarily PD = 8 and the perimeter is 27.

Therefore, the answer is 27.

  (PA)(PC) = (PB)(PD)  and  DA = 2·AB,  CD = 2·BC.

In our problem PA = 4, PB = 5, and PC = 10 so that

Then one may prove (by “chasing angles” and applying the sine–law in the four triangles determined by P and the vertices) that

  AB = 4,  BC = 5,  CD = 10,  DA = 8.

(In one solution one shows that if the equal–angle conditions
  ∠PAB = ∠PDA, ∠PAD = ∠PDC, ∠PBA = ∠PCB, ∠PBC = ∠PCD
are written in “spiral–similarity language” then the similarity taking triangle PAB to triangle PDA sends A to D and so
  DA/AB = PD/PA = 8/4 = 2,
and similarly the similarity taking triangle PBC to triangle PCD gives
  CD/BC = PC/PB = 10/5 = 2.)
Then the perimeter of ABCD is

  AB + BC + CD + DA = 4 + 5 + 10 + 8 = 27.

Thus, the answer is 27.

A sample solution

  (3) ∠PBA = ∠PCB,  (4) ∠PBC = ∠PCD.

One may show that these conditions imply that the spiral–similarity with center P which carries ray PA to ray PD sends A to D and (because the “angle–preserving” maps send lines to lines) carries side AB to side DA. In other words,
  DA/AB = PD/PA.
Likewise, the spiral–similarity carrying PB to PC sends B to C so that
  CD/BC = PC/PB.
Now, applying the sine–law in triangles PAB and PDA we find
  AB = (PA·sin(∠PAB+∠PBA))/sin(∠PBA)
and
  DA = (PA·sin(∠PAD+∠PDA))/sin(∠PDA).
But the equalities (1) and (2) allow one to show that
  sin(∠PAB+∠PBA) = sin(∠PDA+∠PAD).
Thus the ratio DA/AB equals PD/PA. In our problem PA = 4 and (after a short calculation using the “angle–sums about P”) one may show that PD = (PA·PC)/(PB); that is,
  PD = (4·10)/5 = 8.
Then
  DA = 2·AB.
A similar argument shows that
  CD = 2·BC.
But a second application of the sine–law in triangles PAB and PBC shows that
  AB = 4  and  BC = 5.
Thus,
  DA = 8  and  CD = 10.
So the perimeter is
  AB + BC + CD + DA = 4 + 5 + 10 + 8 = 27.
–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––

Therefore, the perimeter of ABCD is 27.

Then the perimeter of ABCD is

In our problem PA = 4, PB = 5, PC = 10 so that if one can prove the “ratio–equalities” implied by

  ∠PAB = ∠PDA,  ∠PAD = ∠PDC,  ∠PBA = ∠PCB,  ∠PBC = ∠PCD

one may show in particular that

  PA/PD = PB/PC.

Thus
  PD = (PC·PA)/PB = (10·4)/5 = 8.

Then
  Perimeter = (4 + 10) + (5 + 8) = 14 + 13 = 27.

A brief discussion of one way to arrive at the “key” ratio is as follows. (There are several approaches; one may use spiral–similarity ideas or trigonometry.)

Introduce the notations

  α = ∠PAB = ∠PDA,
  β = ∠PBA = ∠PCB,
  γ = ∠PAD = ∠PDC,
  δ = ∠PBC = ∠PCD.

Then one may check that the angles of quadrilateral ABCD are
  A = α + γ, B = β + δ, C = β + δ, D = α + γ.
In particular, ABCD is “isosceles” (its opposite angles are equal).

Now one may show that the equalities above imply the existence of two spiral similarities with center P:
 (1) one carrying A to D and B to C, and 
 (2) one carrying A to C and D to B.
A standard property of spiral similarities is that the ratio of the distances from P to the corresponding vertices is preserved. In particular, from (1) one deduces
  PA/PD = PB/PC.
Since PA = 4, PB = 5 and PC = 10 it follows that PD = (10·4)/5 = 8.

A somewhat more detailed (but elementary) trigonometric analysis shows that in fact
  AB + CD = PA + PC  and  BC + DA = PB + PD.
Thus the perimeter is
  (4 + 10) + (5 + 8) = 27.

Therefore, the answer is 27.

We will show that if an interior point P of a convex quadrilateral ABCD satisfies

  (1) ∠PAB = ∠PDA,
  (2) ∠PAD = ∠PDC,
  (3) ∠PBA = ∠PCB, and 
  (4) ∠PBC = ∠PCD,

then one may prove that the “spiral‐similarity relations” force

  PA·PC = PB·PD          (so that PD = (PA·PC)/PB)
  and
  AB + BC + CD + DA = PA + PB + PC + PD.

In our problem PA = 4, PB = 5, and PC = 10 so that
  PD = (4·10)/5 = 8     and Perimeter = 4 + 5 + 10 + 8 = 27.

A short “explanation‐outline” is as follows.

Suppose the rays PA, PB, PC, PD make the four triangles PAB, PBC, PCD, and PDA. One may check that the equalities (1)–(4) imply that the spiral similarity carrying ray PA to ray PD (with center P) takes side AB to side DA and that the spiral similarity carrying ray PB to ray PC takes side BC to side CD. A short (but not entirely “miraculous”) computation using the sine–law in these four triangles shows that
  PA/sin(∠PBA) = PB/sin(∠PAB)
and
  PD/sin(∠PDC) = PC/sin(∠PBC).
Then, using (1) and (3) one may prove that
  PA·PC = PB·PD.
A similar (but even easier) argument shows that
  AB + BC + CD + DA = PA + PB + PC + PD.
Thus the perimeter is determined by the three given lengths.

In our numerical situation the answer is

  4 + 5 + 10 + (4·10/5) = 4 + 5 + 10 + 8 = 27.

Therefore, the perimeter of ABCD is 27.

An answer in brief: 27.

We will show that under the “equal‐angle” conditions the four given distances “control” the side‐lengths in a very neat way. In fact one may prove that if an interior point P of convex quadrilateral ABCD satisfies

  (1) ∠PAB = ∠PDA  and  (2) ∠PAD = ∠PDC
  (3) ∠PBA = ∠PCB  and  (4) ∠PBC = ∠PCD

then one may show that

  • PA·PC = PB·PD                            (★)
  • AB = PA + PB,  BC = PB + PC,  CD = PC + PD,  DA = PD + PA.

A short “explanation” is as follows. (There are several ways to prove these facts; one may use spiral–similarity arguments or “inversion‐plus‐angle–chasing”.) For example, the equalities (1) and (2) imply that the circles (PAB) and (PDA) are tangent at A; a standard homothety then shows that the “turning” from PA to AB equals the turning from PD to DA. In a similar way the equalities (3) and (4) imply that the circles (PBA) and (PCB) are tangent at B. One may then show that the spiral similarity with center P which carries A to D and B to C has the same dilation factor in both cases; that is,
  PD/PA = PC/PB.
In other words, (★) holds. Then one may “chase” the angles in triangles PAB, PBC, PCD, and PDA to prove that
  AB = PA + PB, BC = PB + PC, CD = PC + PD, DA = PD + PA.
(There are several ways to check these formulas; one may use the sine–law in each of the four triangles and use the fact that the “vertex–angles” of ABCD come in equal pairs.)

Now suppose that
  PA = 4, PB = 5, PC = 10.
Then (★) gives
  4·10 = 5·PD  ⟹  PD = 8.
Then the four sides are
  AB = 4 + 5 = 9,
  BC = 5 + 10 = 15,
  CD = 10 + 8 = 18,
  DA = 8 + 4 = 12.
Thus the perimeter is
  9 + 15 + 18 + 12 = 54.

An answer in brief:
  Perimeter = 2(PA + PB + PC + PD) = 2(4 + 5 + 10 + 8) = 54.

Therefore, the perimeter of ABCD is 54.

We will show that under the “equal‐angle” conditions the four distances from P to the vertices “add up” in a very nice way. In fact, one may prove that

  PA·PC = PB·PD        (1)

so that, with PA = 4, PB = 5 and PC = 10, we must have

  PD = (PA·PC)/PB = (4·10)/5 = 8.

A more “miraculous” fact (which you may verify by a careful angle–chasing and use of spiral–similarity) is that when an interior point P of a convex quadrilateral ABCD satisfies

  ∠PAB = ∠PDA,  ∠PAD = ∠PDC,  ∠PBA = ∠PCB,  and ∠PBC = ∠PCD,
  
then one may show that the four sides “combine” so that

  AB + BC + CD + DA = PA + PB + PC + PD.
  
In our problem the four given distances are 4, 5, 10, and (by (1)) 8 so that

  Perimeter = 4 + 5 + 10 + 8 = 27.

A short outline of one way to prove the “miracle” is as follows. One may show that the equal–angle conditions imply that the spiral similarity with center P that carries ray PA to ray PD has ratio

  k = PD/PA = PC/PB.
  
(In our numbers k = 8/4 = 10/5 = 2.) In other words, P “sends” A to D and B to C by the same rotation–dilation. In particular, if you write the sides in “two ways” (using the sine–law in triangles PAB, PBC, PCD, and PDA) you will find that
  CD = 2·AB  and  BC = 2·DA.
Then one easily checks that
  AB + BC + CD + DA = (AB + DA) + (BC + CD)
             = (AB + DA) + 2(AB + DA) = 3(AB + DA).
A short computation shows that in fact
  AB + DA = PA + PD  and  BC + CD = PB + PC.
Thus the perimeter equals (PA + PD) + (PB + PC) = PA + PB + PC + PD.

(There are several ways to “discover” and prove these facts; many authors have used spiral–similarity arguments to show that in a quadrilateral with an “isogonal” point P the perimeter equals PA + PB + PC + PD.)

Thus, with PA = 4, PB = 5, PC = 10 and PD = 8 the perimeter is

  4 + 5 + 10 + 8 = 27.

The final answer is 27.

We will show that under the stated conditions the four “cevian‐lengths”
  PA, PB, PC, PD
(from the interior point P to the vertices A, B, C, D of the cyclic quadrilateral ABCD) satisfy

  (PA)(PC) = (PB)(PD).

In particular, if PA = 4, PB = 5, and PC = 10 then
  PD = (PA·PC)/(PB) = (4·10)/5 = 8.

A somewhat surprising (but true) fact about this configuration is that one may prove
  AB + BC + CD + DA = PA + PB + PC + PD.
In other words, the perimeter of ABCD equals the sum of the four distances from P to the vertices.

One may show (using “spiral‐similarity” arguments and the sine–law in the four triangles PAB, PBC, PCD, and DAP) that the given angle–equalities

  ∠PAB = ∠PDA, ∠PAD = ∠PDC, ∠PBA = ∠PCB, ∠PBC = ∠PCD

force ABCD to be cyclic and, in addition, imply that
  (PA)(PC) = (PB)(PD)
and
  AB + BC + CD + DA = PA + PB + PC + PD.
(There exist several solutions; one may “chase” angles and use the sine–law in the four triangles determined by P and the sides of ABCD.)

Thus, with PA = 4, PB = 5, PC = 10 and PD = 8 the perimeter is

  4 + 5 + 10 + 8 = 27.

So the answer is 27.

Below is one way to explain the key ideas.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
A sample solution outline:

(1) First one shows that the equalities
  ∠PAB = ∠PDA and ∠PAD = ∠PDC
imply that the angles at A and D “split” in the same ratio. Similarly, 
  ∠PBA = ∠PCB and ∠PBC = ∠PCD
show a corresponding relation at B and C. A short angle–chase then shows that
  ∠A + ∠C = 180°,
so that ABCD is cyclic.

(2) Next one shows that if one writes the sine–law in triangles PAB and DAP then
  PA/sin(∠PBA) = PB/sin(∠PAB)
and
  PD/sin(∠PAD) = PA/sin(∠PDA).
Since ∠PAB = ∠PDA the two relations “fit together” (and a similar treatment works at B and C) to yield
  (PA)(PC) = (PB)(PD).

(3) Finally one may prove that in any cyclic quadrilateral with diagonals meeting at an interior point P satisfying (PA)(PC) = (PB)(PD) one has
  AB + BC + CD + DA = PA + PB + PC + PD.
A proof may be given by writing each side (say, AB) in terms of PA, PB and the sine of the appropriate angle (using the sine–law in triangle PAB) and then using the fact that the “split‐angles” at A and D are equal. (There are several variations.)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Thus, with PA = 4, PB = 5, PC = 10 and PD = 8 the perimeter is

  4 + 5 + 10 + 8 = 27.

Answer: 27.

An interested reader is encouraged to work out the details of the spiral–similarity and sine–law arguments.
